name: Places for Play: Playability of Street Views (Boston)
description:
Method replication: same task and rating scale as the paper; the images are not the paper's stimuli (new Google Street View views of Boston, © Google). Kruse, Kang, Liu, Zhang & Gao (2021, Computers, Environment and Urban Systems 90:101693) asked Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to classify street view images by how playable the place is for children, then trained a deep-learning model on the labels to map neighbourhood playability in Boston, Seattle and San Francisco. Regressions found that higher traffic speeds and crime rates go with lower playability, higher perceived beauty with higher playability, and that a lively place is not necessarily playable.

What participants do: after consent, they see 20 Boston street views one at a time, drawn at random from 65, and for each choose one of five categories: very unplayable, unplayable, neither playable nor unplayable, playable, very playable. As in the paper, "playable" is not defined. An attention check, age, gender and whether they look after children follow.

Analysis as in the paper: mean playability per image (the paper aggregated worker labels per image), then image scores related to street features such as traffic, greenery and perceived beauty.

Differences from the original study: (1) the images are 65 new Google Street View views (2017–2026) from random points across Boston, not the paper's labelled image set; (2) the paper covered three cities, this template only Boston; (3) the question on looking after children is an addition. The earlier version of this template showed 4 photographs cropped from the paper PDF.
